directions.novelty_line: **Novelty:** known. Coherent and stochastic error together on superconducting processors are in print: Hashim et al. 2021 (PRX 11, 041039; arXiv 2010.00215, read in full) measured coherent error as 2.0 to 2.9 × 10⁻² of 3.3 to 4.4 × 10⁻² CNOT infidelity on four AQT@LBNL transmons, with the tune-up drifting between experiments, Carignan-Dugas et al. 2024 (Quantum 8, 1367; arXiv 2303.09945) a Z/ZZ-only coherent part beside a larger decoherent part on three IBM chips, and Seif et al. 2024 (ISCA; arXiv 2403.06852) correlated coherent ZZ on IBM ECR devices. ng-p3-18's fresh-job reading (both terms beyond the IBM-calibrated simulator's state on 2 of 3 ibm_fez pairs, blur alone on the third) is the same statement in the same direction on a Heron r2 device, and a replication of our own ng-p3-5c, not a finding about chips; no paper found fits nested rotation and blur terms to Heron tomography across two jobs, which is a method, not a result. Search: WebSearch "Heron processor residual ZZ crosstalk coherent error Pauli twirling ibm_fez OR ibm_torino OR ibm_kingston", "readout error miscalibration mistaken for decoherence two-qubit state tomography superconducting", "Pauli twirling Bell state tomography IBM coherent error twirled versus untwirled" (2026-11-05), arXiv HTML for each lead; claude-opus-5-5, fresh reader subagent of the 2026-11-05c remap.

directions.question: If we randomly scramble the chip's two-qubit operations, the standard fix for steady errors, does the steady kind of error disappear from our entangled qubit pairs?
known: Our results: the steady (rotation) and random (blur) kinds were both needed on two of three pairs on 5 November (ng-p3-18) and on all three on 3 November (ng-p3-5c); scrambling moved program 1's circuit on 4 November, but that bet could not be scored (ng-p3-2, untestable).

The literature: scrambling turns steady errors into random ones on a Berkeley transmon chip (Hashim et al. 2021), and IBM chips' steady error is mostly of the two-qubit ZZ kind (Carignan-Dugas et al. 2024); nobody has done this on a Heron chip's entangled pairs.
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend about 36 seconds of chip time to find out whether randomly scrambling the chip's two-qubit operations, a standard trick for turning steady errors into random ones, makes the steady kind of error disappear from our entangled qubit pairs? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the steady kind of error is gone with scrambling on at least two pairs where it shows up without scrambling)?
directions.hit_means: With scrambling, the steady kind of error is no longer needed on at least two of the pairs that need it without scrambling.

questions_closed.question: Why did program 1's circuit read 0.502 on the chip on the afternoon of 3 November, against about 0.26 predicted?
questions_closed.diagnosis: In every run since (4 and 5 November), putting back the barrier, changing how the shots were grouped, and running the circuit alone in its own job each left the chip at about 30% 'yes', and a better-built simulator did not explain the gap either, so we ruled those out; we could not rule out that the chip itself was different that afternoon (its calibration, drift, or something IBM's servers did that day), because that afternoon cannot be run again.
